en: [The definition is] by virtue of its subsisting in that locus of the absence of the upādhi which is the locus of that property [in question], through the deviation of the upādhi from that property.
However, in cases such as "Air is perceptible because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), the property of knowability...

One should observe that [the definition] is non-deviant with respect to perceptibility in external substances because it is non-deviant with respect to manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), and so forth. Now, an objection: is there not over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*)?

And it is not the case that this [subject-otherness] is itself the object of definition (*lakṣya*), because the delimiting factor of the object of definition (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) has been demonstrated by the root-text beginning with "those which [reside] in a single locus," and so on.

Because [the reason] is absent there, and because deviation from the "other-than-the-pakṣa" (pakṣetaratva) is possible only by taking the pakṣa itself as the locus, whereas deviation from the probandum (sādhya) is impossible by taking that [pakṣa] as the locus, he says: "not led by sublation" (bādhānunnīta). [He says] "because it would be self-contradictory" (svavyāghātakatvāt) regarding the mere presence of a limiting condition (upādhi).

The meaning is that [the reason] would be both a defeater (*dūṣaka*) and a subverter (*vyāghātaka*). The point is that if "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) were a limiting condition (*upādhi*), then since such a condition could exist in every inference, it would follow that all inference is abolished;
consequently, it would be impossible for a limiting condition—which depends on the inference of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—to function as a defeater.

[Objection: But surely there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion of the probandum by that which is to be excluded; in that case, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) is unavoidable. To this, he says: "But that which is inferred by sublation... The meaning is: that which is inferred by sublation (*bādha*)—that is, determined as being a pervader of the probandum—on the grounds that the subject possesses the absence of the probandum.

"Even one whose adjunct (*upādhi*) is doubtful": the sense is that, because there is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), it is possible for there to be doubt regarding the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*) in the case of "otherness of the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*). Nor [should it be argued] that, since it cannot be raised as an objection simply because it is not an adjunct due to its being self-contradictory, it is merely a matter of traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*).

It should not be said that the statement of its being the cause is inconsistent; for where there is the application of a *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) that grasps the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*), there, since the deviation of the pervader necessarily entails the deviation of the pervaded, [the former] possesses the nature of being an inferent of deviation.

Because there is no possibility of contradiction regarding its being a defeater (*dūṣakatva*). He states the view of those who maintain that the defeater-status of a *upādhi* consists in its being a raiser of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*)—namely, "some, however" (*kecit tu*). "And thus" (*itthaṃ ca*) means: and when [the *upādhi*] functions as a defeater by way of raising a counter-argument. And "in this case" (*atra ca*) refers to the position that it is a raiser of a counter-argument.

Regarding the phrase "subsisting in the subject" (*pakṣavṛtti*): the sense is that if it were to subsist in the subject, one could not establish the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the subject due to the absence [of the reason] there.

According to the Guru’s view, worldly speech is non-informative (*anuvādaka*), while only Vedic speech is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in order to refute that position, he says "Vedic," etc. Here, for one who desires heaven...

It should be understood that since the subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) consists in being the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and so forth, the relation is established specifically by that [word]. Regarding the phrase "the object of the intended meaning" (*tātparyaviṣaya*): here, in cases such as "knowledge [resides] in a Brāhmaṇa," when the intended meaning is the relation of locus (*ādhikaraṇatva*), then...

To exclude other possible objects through relations such as being the object [of a cognition], "being the intended object" (*tātparyaviṣayatva*) is a qualifier for the relation. Since the other word-meaning enters into the knowledge of the intention (*tātparya-jñāna*) by way of being the other word-meaning, a relation with that which is remembered as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth is not established; therefore—

Regarding the term "smārita" (recalled): the state of being recalled is to be understood through the function (*vṛtti*) [of the word]. Consequently, there is no deficiency even if a relation is not established with the form presented by the word *vastu* (entity) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and so forth. And in the case of the reason, as in the example: "This son of the king comes."

In cases such as "Let the man be removed," there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because the probandum is absent in the portion "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), due to the absence of *tātparya* regarding the connection between the two compatible meanings, "king" and "man. Therefore, the qualification of "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) is [necessary]. And this [expectancy] consists in this word [being] with this [word].

The purport of a word is that it should produce a cognition of its own meaning as connected with the meanings of other words through association with such-and-such [words]. Therefore, there is no contingency of the other parts being useless due to the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). This applies even in sentences such as "sprinkle with fire" (*vaḍdhinā siñcati*).

The term "yogyatā" (semantic competency) is included in the reason (*hetu*) in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by the absence of the probandum— namely, being preceded by a valid cognition of the connection— in cases such as "the pot is blue" and "the cloth is a substance. This is because semantic competency and expectancy exist between "blue" and "cloth" within the portion of that sentence, namely "the cloth is blue."

The term "asati" (in the absence of) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because of the existence of causality; and the term "kadamba" is for the purpose of obtaining the mutual correlative relationship (*parasparapratiyogitva*) among expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and the other factors. Otherwise, since the probandum (*sādhya*) would consist of mutually dependent meanings, there would be the undesirable consequence of deviation.

But surely, since a cognition that has as its qualificandum the object of activity and as its qualifier the property that delimits desirability is the motivator [of action], and since the inference [in question]— which has as its content the fact of being preceded by a cognition of a relation— is not of such a nature, how can it be a motivator?
For an inference is necessarily characterized by a qualifier that delimits the pervasion.

Even though the status of being preceded by valid cognition (*pramā*) is established by the fact that [the cognition] is preceded by valid cognition, since a cognition having "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) as its qualifier and the object in front (*purovartin*) as its qualificandum does not arise from that [inference], the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is accepted for that purpose; hence he says: "Or else... (*yadvā*).
Regarding the phrase "mutual connection" (*mithaḥsaṃsarga*): the meaning is that they possess a mutual connection which is the object of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*).

By this, there is no shift of the subject matter (*arthāntara*) by taking up a connection that is not the object of the intention. Now, one might ask: since the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), how can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) be grasped? To this he says: "Even in the example... (*dṛṣṭānte 'pi*).

[Objection: Surely, since the effect in the form of an inference must be accounted for elsewhere, the knowledge of pervasion (vyāptijñāna) must be postulated immediately following the hearing of the word in every case. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (kiṃca). "Having postulated the cognition of the word" means having postulated the recollection of the word. By the word "padajñāna" and so forth, [the author] implies the object itself.

The point is that since the recollection of words such as "jar" can also occur through an object in the form of a jar and so forth, the relationship of being a signifier (*vācakatva*)—just like the relationship of being the signified (*vācyatva*)—also possesses the capacity to cause recollection.
This is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood that this implies the postulation of the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth.

In the inference: "These word-meanings, such as the gem-maker and so forth, possess mutual connection because they are presented by words possessing semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and so on," semantic competency is not a qualifier of the logical mark (*liṅga*),
since only a certain logical mark can be a means of ascertainment.

Furthermore, since verbal cognition is observed even when there is doubt regarding the competency [of the words], they maintain that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is a means of knowledge distinct [from inference]. However, the Miśras argue that if the word conveys meaning by way of inference, then in the case of "Bring the jar," the jar is the object, bringing is the action, and the effort is the agent; thus, the sentence is merely formally capable (*svarūpayogya*).
It cannot be argued that [the cognition] is "unfit for its own nature," because inference is possible in both cases.
Nor should it be said that there is no inference there due to the absence of a cause constituted by semantic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*),
for inference can occur through a misconception of expectancy, and because that [inference] is not sublated with respect to its object.

They say that because it possesses the nature of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a word that is authoritative does not, by its very nature, produce a cognition [of such a relation]. Others, however, maintain that in cases such as "distinct from the pot" (*ghaṭāt pṛthak*),
there is a qualificandumness (*viśeṣyatā*) that is non-limited (*aniravacchinna*) with respect to the mode (*prakāra*) of distinctness having the pot as its limit (*avadhi*).

The verbal cognition of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) as having a substratum is established by universal experience; and for us, this is accounted for because the knowledge of words possessing such a sequence is the cause of such a verbal cognition. For the Vaiśeṣikas, however, distinctness [is understood] as being delimited by the jar (*ghaṭāvadhika*).
This cannot be established by the inference: "because it is recalled by a distinct word that is expectancy-laden with the word 'jar'";
for although distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) appears as a property of the subject (*pakṣa*), its substratum does not appear [in that cognition].
Nor can it be established by taking a cloth as the subject and inferring: "the cloth possesses distinctness relative to a jar."

It must be stated that this [objection] is resolved: because the qualificand-ness (viśeṣyatā) residing in the cloth and so forth is delimited by "cloth-ness" (paṭatva), which serves as the delimitor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka) in that case,
there is no identity of form with such a verbal cognition that possesses an undelimited (niravacchinna) qualificand-ness.

"Nevertheless, because [the definition] is not sustained, they say so"—this is the direction [of the argument]. (140–141) Among those [definitions], "having a non-existent object of negation" means having a probandum (*sādhya*) that is not the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*).
This is because, according to the literal reading, there would be the contradiction of both proof and non-proof. And regarding the state of not being the counter-positive of an absolute absence...

The application of the definition [of existence] occurs because [the property of] being an object of valid cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth exists [in all things]. Nor should it be argued that this is impossible because that [property], in its nature as being the object of a valid cognition (*pramā*), is manifold and thus lacks a commonality;
for validity itself (*pramātva*) is indeed common [to all instances] through a transitive relation (*paramparā-sambandha*). And thus:

Even when there is the error that [the property of] being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and so forth is negative-only (*vyatirekin*), it should be understood that it is indeed purely positive-only (*kevalānvayin*). Regarding the phrase "having no similar instances" (*asatsapakṣa*):
because of the contradiction between [its] establishment and non-establishment, here too [the reason] is one whose concomitance with the probans has not been apprehended.

That which has a probandum (sādhya) that is non-occurrent-in-the-counter-example (vyatireki) is to be understood as having "the state of being the cause" (tatkatva) as its meaning. "Possessing a similar instance" (satsapakṣa) means:

that which has a probandum whose positive and negative concomitances have been apprehended. "By whatever relation, that which is delimited by whatever [property]" refers to the pervasion (vyāpakatā) as determined by the pervasiveness (vyāpyatā) delimited by a specific form and delimited by a specific relation.

The meaning is "it is apprehended. Regarding the phrase "pervasion by the other" (*itaravyāpyatā*), the meaning is "the state of being pervaded by the other. In the reading "pervasion of the other by way of identity" (*tādātmyenetaravyāpakatā*), the meaning is "the state of being a pervader residing in the other, as delimited by the relation of identity. [This refers to] "by way of the relation of identity."

The meaning is that an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a relation of identity (tādātmya) is established. For if it were not stated by which relation pervasion (vyāpyatā) is apprehended, then the establishment of the absolute absence of one thing would occur wherever the pervasiveness of the other is apprehended through the relation of identity.

The term "existence" (bhāvaḥ) is used with restriction, meaning "by means of an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of conjunction" (saṃyoga-sambandhāvaccchinna-pratiyogitāka-ghaṭābhāvena). By this,
it is restricted to mean "by means of an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by that [specific] relation."

By this, it is meant with emphasis that [the non-existence] is by way of an absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by that specific relation; the meaning is that its establishment does not occur by way of an absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by another relation. And by this, it is shown that the pervasion is grasped by whichever relation [is operative].

The fruit of this has been indicated; by the very method already shown, the purpose of the two expressions "in whatever form" and "delimited by which" is also to be inferred. Now, one might object: "Since there is an absence of knowledge regarding the co-presence of the probandum and the probans, how can there be knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)? To this, he says: "And here... and so forth. And thus:

The point is that since the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) occurs through negative co-presence (*vyatirekasahacāra*) alone, there is no dependence on the apprehension of positive co-presence (*anvayasahacāra*). [Objection: But surely, without the prior establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*), its absence cannot be known, and thus the negative concomitance would be difficult to apprehend.

If it is argued that [the proof] results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) once the probandum (*sādhya*) is established, we say no. Since the probandum is already established by perception in the case of a jar and so forth, there is no *siddhasādhana*, because the intended cognition—that earth is distinct from things other than itself—is not yet established. It is only when the delimiters of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) are multiple that there is *siddhasādhana* in part.

Because it is a fault. For this very reason, in the case of the [inference] "Speech and mind are non-eternal," since the non-eternality of the cognition "speech" (which is the subject of the thesis) is already established, there is no *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already proven) even in part. Now, one might object: even so, how can a jar be the subject (*pakṣa*) with respect to the probandum?

If it is argued that this is not so because there is certainly an absence of both doubt regarding that [object] and the desire to prove it, we say no; for the doubt— "Is the entire earth different from others or not?"— and the desire to prove it in that manner have the jar as their object, and thus, when a specific perception occurs in the form of "jar-ness" or when there is proof [of the conclusion], it occurs in that very form.

Doubt and the desire to prove [the probandum] do not belong to you, whereas they certainly belong to you in the case of "earth-ness. Now, one might object: since the difference from others is established through positive concomitance (anvaya) alone—namely, "Earth is different from what is other than itself because it possesses earth-ness, like a jar"—the negative inference (vyatirekin) is redundant. This is not so, because the positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti) has not been grasped.

Since it is possible for a negative inference (*vyatirekyanumiti*) to be produced at the stage when the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) becomes manifest, the operation of negative inference proceeds without any obstacle.
He states the view of the Teacher (*ācārya*) with the words "But some [say]... by means of negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*).

By means of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) independent of positive concomitance (*anvaya-sahacāra*), it is stated that "it is only positive pervasion" (*anvaya-vyāptir eva*); the word "only" (*eva*) serves to exclude negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*). Now, one might object: if this is so, how [can there be inference], given the absence of the cause consisting in the cognition of negative pervasion?
Therefore, he says "but not... regarding negative inference (*vyatirekyanumiti*).

The phrase "knowledge of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekavyāptijñāna*) is to be connected with "in the case of inference" (*anumitau*), and so forth. Now, if the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) alone is the cause [of inference], how can there be the conventional usage "negative" (*vyatirekī*)? To this he says: "where... Now...

In cases such as "Earth is distinct from others because it possesses earthness," since the probandum—namely, distinction from others—is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), how can there be a grasp of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*)?
To this, he says: "The establishment of the probandum, however... [Objection: But if the probandum has already been determined in a jar or the like, how...
In that case, there would be an inference of difference from others; therefore, he says "subsequently.

The sense is that when an inference is made with respect to a specific delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not constitute an obstacle. Here...
Furthermore, since the knowledge of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) arises from the knowledge of as many categories as constitute the components of that positive concomitance,

there is no evidence for the claim that the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*) is its cause. Nor does the instrumental suffix in the phrase "by means of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekasahacāreṇa*) denote causality (*prayojakatva*), and that [causality]...
It is not untenable;

for it must be said that the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) serves as the instrumental cause therein by way of removing the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra-śaṅkā*), which is an obstacle to the knowledge of positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*).
Even when there is the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*), the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra-śaṅkā*) in another locus remains just as it was; therefore,
[the apprehension of negative concomitance] functions there by way of removing the suspicion of deviation pertaining to that specific locus.

Nor is its utility [established] by that alone; for the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that locus is removed merely by apprehending the absence of the probans (*sādhana*) in that locus. This lack of conviction is indicated by the phrase "they say" (*vadanti*). ||142||143|| Some Mīmāṃsakas [hold this view].

That too—namely, that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa* [other than inference])—[is rejected]. [For example, in the case of the statement: "He does not eat during the day."

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), the statement "the peacock does not dance on anything other than a mountain, yet it dances [on a mountain]" is included. Now, one might object: from this sentence, the cognition "the peacock dances on the mountain" arises; however, such a cognition is not possible through its negative counterpart (*vyatireka*), namely, the dancing on a mountain [in the absence of the mountain].

If it is argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) must be a distinct means of knowledge because it establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, we say no. For example: "The peacock's dance has the mountain as its locus, because, while not having any locus other than the mountain, it does have a locus."

Because the cognition of a peacock dancing on a mountain can occur through a purely positive-negative (anvaya-vyatirekin) inference alone, such as "like the state of being a mountain" [144]. Regarding the phrase "as a property" (*dharmatvena*):
this is stated according to the view of the ancients; however, in the view of the moderns, [the definition is] "eternal consciousness, bliss..."

It should be understood that, according to the Śruti "Brahma is bliss," since the Blessed Lord is established as eternal bliss, the delimitor of dharma’s effect is either the state of being produced-bliss (janyasukhatva) or a sub-class of the genus "bliss" (sukhatva). In that regard,
between those two [alternatives], it is precisely because the knowledge of the fruit is the cause for the desire for the fruit.

"Puruṣārtha is possible" means that pleasure and the absence of pain are possible as the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Now, one might object: the meaning of the phrase "that which is known," and so forth, is "being the object of a desire produced by a cognition whose content is itself."

Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the means (*upāya*), since that too is the object of a desire produced by the cognition that it is a means to achieve what is desired with respect to its own object; therefore, he says: "the desire for something other [than the object]."

146 || Regarding the phrase "the cognition of being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*): Now, there is no evidence for the view that the cognition of being achievable through effort is an independent cause of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).

[For] a cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*), whose qualificandum is delimited by a particular property (*taddharmāvacchinnaviśeṣyaka*), [is the cause] of a desire whose qualifier is that same property (*taddharmaprakārakecchā*).

If it is argued that [the desire to act] arises from the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end, where the qualificandum is delimited by being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*), because the causal role [of such knowledge] is already established— [we reply: no, for there are cases where the fact of being a means to a desired end is not apprehended as being "achievable through effort" (i.e.,
*kṛtisādhya-pākatvena*), but rather simply as "being cooked" (*śuddha-pākatvena*).

When the state of being achievable by an effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) are apprehended as pure cooking (*śuddhapākatvena*), since an inclination toward cooking is observed even there, a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is also necessarily required in accordance with that observation; therefore, for the sake of establishing that [desire], the cognition of being achievable by an effort must exist independently.

This is because causality [of such knowledge] is necessary. Now, if it is argued that there is no evidence for the claim that the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is a cause of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), since the desire to act does not arise regarding rain and the like precisely because the knowledge of being unachievable through effort (*akṛtisādhyatājñāna*) acts as an obstacle—[we reply: this is not so.

Because it is simpler (lāghava) to posit that the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the cause [of action], rather than positing the obstructive nature of the cognitions of the absence of being achievable through effort, its pervasion (*vyāpya*), and the property that delimits it (*tadavacchedakadharma*).

Regarding "the cognition of being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*): otherwise, even when there is a cognition of fruitlessness, [one would still act] in the case of bowing to a *caitya* and so forth.

The state of being a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is the [resulting] disposition (*bhāva*). Here, this should be understood: when the knowledge that cooking is a means to a desired end has "being an object of action" (*kāryatā*) as its delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), the delimiting property of the desire to act directed toward cooking and so forth is not simply "the state of being a desire to act," provided that "having the property of being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatvaprakārakatva*) is included [in the definition].

Because there is an absence of a purpose [in that case], and because it would follow that the desire "May cooking arise" is not included, [the definition] is rather: "The state of being a desire whose primary qualificandum is delimited by the property of cooking (pākatva). The term "primary" (mukhya) is included to avoid over-extension (vyabhicāra) to the desire "May happiness, which is to be accomplished by cooking, arise."

In the expression "being a means to what is desired" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), desire (*icchā*) is the qualifier by virtue of its mere existence (*svarūpasatī*). Therefore, even at a time when there is no knowledge of desire, the fulfillment of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is maintained. For this very reason, it is precisely because the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is the cause [of action]. (147) Regarding "intensely disliked" (*balavaddviṣṭa*): "disliked" (*dviṣṭa*) refers to that which has become the object of aversion (*dveṣaviṣayībhūta*).

And aversion [arises] toward suffering from the cognition of it as being such [i.e., as suffering], and toward a snake and so forth from the cognition of them as being the means to that [suffering]. Intensity in aversion is a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*). [The phrase "is an obstacle" (*pratibandhakam*) means: But [one might object]:
if the non-cognition of the state of being a means to the object of intense aversion is the obstacle, then...
When Caitra possesses a powerful aversion toward engaging in sexual intercourse with an unapproachable woman (*agamyā*), then for Maitra—
who is devoid of such aversion but who possesses the knowledge that such intercourse is a means to that same hell—
the occurrence of desire and activity [toward that act] would be impossible. This is likewise the case for Caitra himself at a later time.

Even when such aversion exists, it is not postulated that the cognition of being produced by something intensely disliked at that time by that person acts as an inhibitor with respect to the desire or the volitional effort of that person at that time, provided that for that person at that time there is no [such cognition] anywhere.
It should not be argued that, because hatred is included within that person at that specific time, its status as an obstacle to such a cognition is not postulated;

and thus, since there is no established instance of such an obstacle, the cause consisting of its absence would be non-existent, leading to the impossibility of purposeful action (*pravṛtti*). For [this applies only] to the case of a particular person...

When there is intense aversion toward hell resulting from approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*), then, because that person has no desire for it at that time, the desire of that person directed toward the object of approaching a forbidden woman at that specific time is unestablished;
consequently, since such a causal relationship (between the desire and the action) does not exist when that person and that time are included, [the objection] does not apply there.

If it is argued that [the cause is] the owner of the famine who acts as the motivator for the non-arising of the desire to engage in forbidden sexual intercourse with a woman belonging to that [same] man—

[we reply: no, because there is no such undesirable consequence (āpatti) once one postulates that the cognition of a thing's being a producer, qualified by a hatred whose qualifier is that property, acts as an inhibitor in that case.

In the case of such a desire that is not preceded by a hatred characterized by that property, the absence of such hatred is the cause; in the case of such a desire for that object which is preceded by such a hatred, the absence of the cognition of its being a producer [of pleasure] as delimited by that property is the cause. This refers to "intense hatred."
When there is a desire for an object such as cooking, a dislike directed toward that same object—produced by the cognition that it is a means to an object of intense aversion—acts as an inhibitor.
This is because, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is simpler than postulating the two previously mentioned inhibitors. Where...
In that [system], it is held that a single action produces both intense pleasure and intense pain;

however, just as in the case of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), there is no arising of desire or aversion therein. According to that view, because of the cognition that it is a means to what is intensely disliked (*balavaddviṣṭasādhanatvajñāna*), aversion is produced in the third moment, and in the moment immediately following that—
It should be stated that for you as well, there is the production of desire; for in that case, the production of desire is desired.

Others say that because a momentary delay must be determined by oath, this indicates a lack of satisfaction [with the previous view]. Regarding the phrase "the cognition that [an action] does not produce a powerful undesirable result": here too...

The refined conclusion to be understood is as follows: for a desire that does not follow from an aversion toward a particular property (taddharmaprakāraka-dveṣa), the cause is the cognition that [the object] is not productive of that which is delimited by that property (taddharmāvacchinna-ajanakatvajñāna);

however, for a desire that does follow from such an aversion, the cause is the absence of that aversion toward that property (taddharmaprakāraka-dveṣābhāva). By the phrase "in the opinion of some" (kasyacinmate) in the root-text, a lack of satisfaction (asvarasa) is indicated.

It has been indicated that the property of being a cognition of the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñānatva*) cannot serve as the delimitor of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka*),

because [the absence of such a result] possesses a qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) relative to an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) consisting in the production of a powerful undesirable result; thus, it is composed of such a relationship between the determined (*nirūpya*) and the determiner (*nirūpaka*).

By virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate that the cause [of action] consists precisely in the absence of the cognition that it is a means to a powerful undesirable end (*balavadaniṣṭasādhanatvajñānābhāva*), rather than in the absence of a certainty regarding its being a non-concomitant with such an end (*tadanubandhitvaniścayābhāva*)—

which would have to be qualified by the absence of a sublation by the cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyajñānānāskandita*). This is because the latter alternative requires the qualification of "not being sublated by the cognition of invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyaniścayānāskandita*) in relation to the cognition that it is not a concomitant with a powerful undesirable end (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna*).

It should not be argued that there is complexity (*gaurava*) in [positing] "being a cognition" (*jñānatva*) as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the state of being an inhibitor (*pratibandhakatā*). For even when there is doubt regarding whether an action such as fighting is a means to a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭasādhanatva*), desire and activity still arise; thus, it must be admitted that only the certainty (*niścaya*) of its being connected with a powerful undesirable result is the inhibitor of desire, while even the doubt (*saṃśaya*) of its *not* being so connected is the cause [of desire]. Consequently, the opposite position would involve greater complexity. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that if the cognition of "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*) were not a motivator for action, then because that object would lack the status of being the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyartha*), sentences such as "One should not eat *kalañja*" would result in being invalid (*aprāmāṇya*). For that cognition [is indeed a motivator].
Even in the absence of being a direct cause of activity,
because it serves as a motivator for activity by way of subverting powerful undesirable means that obstruct activity,
it is the object of the cognition that motivates activity.
Because the status of [the injunction] as having the purpose of enjoining (vidhyarthatva) is not lost. Here, although there may be aversion in the first moment,

desire for the fruit in the second moment, and the cognition of the means to the fruit in the third moment— wherein, due to the destruction of the aversion in the third moment, the desire for the means indeed arises in the fourth moment— in a case where...

The arising of these [desires] occurs through a sequence beginning with the desire for the fruit; therein, due to the absence of the cause consisting of the desire for the fruit, there is no desire for the means, and so it is elsewhere as well, because the simultaneous occurrence of the specific qualities of the self is not admitted. Thus, [there is the absence] of the cognition that [the action] is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence, and of aversion.

Nor is it logical for [the cognition of being unaccompanied by a powerful undesirable consequence] to be an obstructer. Furthermore, while it is not logical for the cognition that something is not connected with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitvajñāna*) to be the cause [of desire], nevertheless,

since it is an empirical fact that desire and activity do not arise even when aversion has been separated by two or three moments, [the cognition of being unconnected with a powerful undesirable consequence must be the cause].

Alternatively, it should be understood that because it is accepted that there is no simultaneity between two cognitions, the previously mentioned status of being an obstructor and the status of being a cause are necessary. (148) By this, [it is meant] with the qualification of "intensity" in relation to aversion. Regarding "activity," etc.: and the nature of activity is...

A specific universal (*jāti*) is established as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for being produced by passion (*rāga*). Likewise, cessation-ness (*nivṛttitva*) is a specific universal established as the delimiting factor for being produced by aversion (*dveṣa*). And the nature of the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoniyatnatva*) is the state of being an effort directed toward the natural movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). ||149||

Now, if the absence of the cognition that [an action] is connected with a powerful undesirable consequence were not a cause for activity, then it would follow that one would engage in eating food mixed with honey and poison; therefore, he says "honey... [and so on].
"Due to the absence of the desire to act" means: with respect to the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
The point is that the cause [of action] is the absence of the cognition that [an act] is followed by a powerful undesirable consequence.

"Like the cognition that it is achievable through effort, etc. means otherwise, even the cognition that it is achievable through effort and so forth would be a cause only for the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and not for the activity of another, because of the intervention of an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*).
The point is that the argument—that the agent's activity is not "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha)—is equally applicable to the case at hand.

He states the Prābhākara view: "the cognition of being an effect. This refers to both [the desire to act and the effort]. "By means of that" means by means of the desire whose qualifier is "being achievable through effort" (kṛtisādhyatva). "Of both alone" [refers to the preceding].

The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also. Regarding the phrase "its own qualification" (*svaviśeṣaṇa*): "its own" refers to the person who is acting; its "qualification" is desire in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), and time, purity, and so forth in the case of a mandatory rite (*nitya*).

The meaning is that there is a connection with those [qualifications] in the alternative [of their presence], and the "recollection" (*pratisandhāna*) of that is the cognition [of it]. Its status as the cause for the cognition of the task to be performed (*kāryatā*) [is established].

By way of inferential knowledge (*liṅgajñāna*). For instance, there is the inference: "Cooking is achievable by my effort, because it exists when my effort is present and does not exist when it is absent, and because it is a means to what I desire. In this case, if one were to state merely that it is "a means to what I desire," there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to rain and the like.

The word "truth" (*satyam*) [is used]. To exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as food cooked by another which serves as a means to my desired end, the phrase "without my effort" (*matkṛtiṃ vinā*) contains the word "my" (*mat-*). To exclude deviation in the case of physical exertion (*śrama*), the phrase "because it is a means to my desired end" (*madiṣṭasādhanatvāt*) is used; for [exertion] is my own exertion.

It cannot be argued that because the enemy of death (Yama) is a means to achieve what is desired, the aforementioned defect remains as it was, and therefore the term "pleasure" (*mad*) must apply there too;

nor can it be said that the knowledge of being achievable by an effort dependent on one's own will is the sole motivator for action, otherwise there would be the consequence of acting toward unavoidable labor, and furthermore, such [a motive] is not established by the inference stated above.

Because being "to-be-accomplished" (sādhyatva) consists precisely in being achievable by an action dependent on one's own will (*svecchādhīna*). And thus, even in the case of the reason, the qualification "dependent on one's own will" must be applied to the phrase "without my action";
otherwise, [the reason would fail] in the case of something desired by another that is to be accomplished by my action for the sake of achieving a desired end.
Because, in cases such as contact with water that is invariably concomitant [with fire], there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This being so,

since it is possible to avoid the fallacy of deviation regarding exertion simply by the absence of a reason constructed according to one's own whim, the purpose of the qualificand portion (*viśeṣyadala*) is indeed not possible.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because it is a different reason (*hetvantara*), just like [the inference of] blue smoke and so forth.

Thus, the inference is: "I am one who performs the *saṃdhyāvandana* as accomplished by my present effort, because, while being a twice-born (*dvijāti*), I possess purity and other qualities at the prescribed time for *saṃdhyā*. One who is a twice-born...

When one possesses the purification and other requirements prescribed for the time of the *saṃdhyā*, there is a general pervasion (*sāmānyato vyāpti*) such that "he [is] a performer of the *saṃdhyāvandana* at that time, which is to be accomplished by an effort at that time.
And even though, in this manner, an inference based on the reason of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is possible regarding the subject (*pakṣa*),...
A cognition of being an effect (*kāryatājñāna*) produced by the non-recognition of [the agent] as possessing his own qualifier is not possible;
for while the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) resides in the sacrifice and thus lacks the status of being a qualifier of the person,
even though desire (*icchā*) is a qualifier of the person, it cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

It should not be argued that even though [the knowledge of being a means] is a constituent of the logical mark (liṅga), it does not bring about the cognition of its possessing that [property] in the subject (pakṣa);

for even the cognition of being a means to what is desired consists, in the case of sacrifices and the like, in the cognition of a connection with desire in the form of being a means to its own object.

In reality, the knowledge of that which possesses the property (tadvat), the knowledge of its relation, or the knowledge of it alone is [the cause], but the subject (pakṣa) is not included therein; thus,
even the knowledge of being a means to a desired end consists in the knowledge of its relation to desire, and therefore consists in the knowledge of that desire.

...because there is no lack of logical consistency. Now, if it is argued that the cognition of being an effect (*kāryatājñāna*)— produced by the non-recognition of [the agent] as possessing his own specific qualifiers— is the motivator [of action],
then even at a time when the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is absent, [there would be motivation] toward cooking.
Where there is an inference of effectness based on another reason composed of its own qualifiers, such as effort and so forth—for example:

"Cooking is achievable by my volition independent of my will, because, while being distinct from fatigue and the like, it is the counter-positive of an absence whose occurrence is necessitated by the absence of my volition"; or alternatively:

Since [an action] would not exist without being subject to one’s own will, there would follow the consequence of activity even in that case; therefore, he says: "For in the case of what is desired" (*kāmye hi*). "Desire" (*kāmanā*) refers to a desire directed toward a sacrifice, cooking, and so forth. In some places, the reading is exactly thus. And so, in the phrase "one’s own qualification" (*svaviśeṣaṇa*), it is specifically that very form of desire which is intended.
Or rather, its own qualification must be stated. Likewise, "possessing a qualification" must also be stated as consisting in being a means for establishing its own object.
Therefore, [the definition does not fail] in the case of the inference of the effect produced by the knowledge of the second reason, such as "not dependent on one's own will," and so forth.
The sense is that this would lead to the occurrence of [unwanted] activity.

Now, if it is argued that the knowledge of being a task (kāryatājñāna) produced by the knowledge of being a means to a desired end leads to the occurrence of activity, then there would be the unwanted consequence of activity toward eating food mixed with honey and poison; therefore, he says: "And from that..."

"Balavadaniṣṭa" means "accompanied by a powerful undesirable [consequence]. Thus, the sense is that when there is no recollection of [the action] as possessing its own qualifier, the qualifier "having for its object the state of not being accompanied by a powerful undesirable [consequence]" must be supplied.
[Objection: But even for one who is already satiated, regarding eating...

Since the occurrence of activity would also follow for him [the one who has already eaten], because there exists a cognition of the object as something to be done (*kāryatājñāna*) produced by a mark (*liṅga*) based on a desire for food at a past time, he says:

"one who is satiated. The meaning is that at that time, desire is not a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the person. And thus, in the phrase "his own qualification" (*svaviśeṣaṇa*), [it is to be understood accordingly].

The intended meaning is that the qualification "being contemporary" (tadānīntanatvam) must be added. Now, an objection may be raised: since there is the possibility of engaging in the Sandhyā-vandana rite based on a cognition of being an effect—produced by the knowledge of a logical mark such as being the counter-positive of an absence whose non-existence is caused by an action dependent on one's own will—then even an action [of one's own] would possess this very qualification; therefore [the definition fails].

He says: "Perpetual purity and so forth. By the word "and so forth," the time for performing those prescribed duties is included. Nor should it be asked how time can be a qualification of a person; for that [time] [qualifies the person] through the relation of being alive, which is its own occurrence.

Because it is a qualification of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇatvāt*), or because [the] word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes such things as living during the prescribed time; thus, in the case of an activity directed toward what is obligatory (*nitya*), by the term "its own qualification," only that qualification existing at that time— such as purity (*śucitva*) and so forth— is to be understood, and not [anything else].

The meaning is that this is the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). The Naiyāyika raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*): "In comparison to that" (*tadapekṣayā*) means in comparison to the knowledge of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*), which is produced by the knowledge of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) qualified by the absence of connection to a more powerful undesired result (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

Regarding the term "by way of parsimony" (*lāghavena*): the sense is that *viṣayatva* (objecthood) is simpler than being produced by [an action] characterized by such constraints as a mandatory rule (*niyama*). Now, one might object: the cognition that something does not produce a powerful undesirable result is not the cause [of activity], because in some cases, even a greater amount of suffering is not considered "powerful" when it is to be accomplished through great effort.

In some cases, because a minor [fault] is powerful, it is difficult to state that the powerlessness of what follows it is itself powerful; therefore, he says: "and being not followed by an undesirable result that is more powerful.
Regarding "the arising of the desired": this refers to the suffering that is inseparable from the arising of the desired.

The meaning is that it is the non-production of that suffering which is distinct from what is expected [from the action]. By this, the objection regarding the occurrence of activity toward eating food mixed with honey and poison is refuted;
for by that [action], there is the production of the suffering of death, which is distinct from the suffering that is inseparable from the arising of the desired [result].

Regarding the phrase "because it produces [pleasure]," some object: "In the case of an action that produces mere pleasure, the suffering that is invariably concomitant with the desired result is not established;
therefore, it follows that there would be no inclination toward such an action. This is incorrect.
According to the maxim "action is painful," there is no lack of establishment because there is an invariable rule that an action producing pleasure also produces suffering.

Others, however, say that the meaning of what was stated is "the state of not being a producer of the suffering of hell which is invariably concomitant with its own arising when mixed [with other acts]"; thus, there is no lack of establishment [of the definition]. But if this were so, one would not engage in such acts as approaching another's wife—which are known to be means for attaining hell—due to the intensity of passion.

Because it is certain that [the action] produces the suffering of hell as an inseparable consequence of the desired [result], he says: "by a powerful aversion. And the powerfulness of the aversion is a specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa*). For this very reason, in the case of one blinded by passion (*rāgāndha*), regarding the suffering produced by approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*) and so forth—
There is no such hatred [toward the means] at that time, nor does activity proceed even toward its cause.

He demonstrates the contradiction between the states of being the goal (*sādhyatva*) and being the means (*sādhanatva*): "For that which is unestablished," etc. This means: of cooking and so forth as qualified by existence in the first moment; "that which is established" means qualified by moments other than the first.

Since "being achievable through effort" (kṛtisādhyatva)— which is constituted by the relation to the moment immediately following the performance of the action— resides in the cooking itself at the very moment the cooking arises;
whereas "being a means to a result such as boiled rice," which occurs at a later time and is constituted by the relation to the moment immediately preceding that rice, [does not reside there].
The meaning is that at the moment of their simultaneous arising, there is no coexistence [of the two], because of the contradiction consisting in their not existing in one place at the same time.
Although...

Since the property of being a means to rice (*odana-sādhanatva*)— defined as possessing a characteristic that delimits its existence in the moment immediately preceding the rice which occurs at a later time— is possible even for cooking (*pāka*) as it exists in its first moment, how can there be a contradiction? Nevertheless, because activity does not arise from the cognition "this is inherently capable [of producing the result], yet it does not actually bring about the result," [the opponent argues that the two cognitions are contradictory].

The point is this: one must state that the cause of activity is the knowledge of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) in the form of "being productive of a result" (*phalopadhāyakatva*), which is common to both certainty and doubt;

however, the aforementioned "productivity of a result" is not possible in the case of a sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth as characterized by its first moment. This addresses the contradiction between the states of being an effect (*sādhyatva*) and being a means (*sādhanatva*).

Having established that it is impossible for those two to be the objects of a single cognition, he says: "Nor can one [cognition] grasp both at once. A cognition that does not apprehend its own respective delimiters (*avacchedaka*) regarding a substance that exists by non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*) is not possible. For example, "the tree is at the root."

Because it is cognized precisely as being "conjoined" [with the agent]. Thus, regarding both the state of being the goal (*sādhyatva*) and the state of being the means (*sādhanatva*), there is the cognition that the unestablished object is the domain of its own respective delimiters—namely, establishedness and non-establishedness—as in the cognitions: "The cooking is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhya*) while unestablished," and "The cooking, being established, is a means to the desired end."

Alternatively, it must be stated that [the cognition] has a collective substratum (samūhālambana) as its form; however, that is not possible because the cognitions of "established" and "unestablished" are mutually contradictory—this is the underlying intention.
Therefore, it is said: "due to the difference in time. For the cooking is currently unestablished.
It should not be argued that activity arises solely from the cognitions "the cooking is achievable through effort," "it will be accomplished in the future," and "it is a means to a desired end";
for the present time and the subsequent time are not mutually inclusive, and [the same applies to] the state of being alive.

Since it is possible to have an inference such as "I am now one who can achieve the act of eating poison, because I possess life," there exists a cognition of task-to-be-accomplished (*kāryatā*)— common even to the case of eating poison—
which is produced by the recognition of oneself as possessing the aforementioned qualification (*svaviśeṣaṇavattāpratisandhāna*).

It must be stated that the knowledge of "taskness" (*kāryatā*)— produced by the recollection of any one of the marks such as being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*), purity (*śauca*), and so forth, which is not followed by a powerful undesired consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhin*)— is the motivator. Compared to that, the knowledge of taskness whose object is being a means to a desired end not followed by a powerful undesired consequence is far more weighty.

With the intention that this very [instrumentality] is postulated as being common to both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites, he refutes the Prābhākara position with the words "not so" (*maivam*). He refutes the contradiction between the states of being an end (*sādhya*) and being a means (*sādhana*) with the words "and not" (*na ca*); the meaning is "for it is not the case. The phrase "at some time or other" (*yadā kadācit*)...
The meaning is that there is no contradiction between being a means (sādhanatva) existing at some time and being something to be accomplished (sādhyatva) existing at some [other] time.

Thus, even though there is a contradiction between being something to be accomplished by an effort (*kṛti*) at one specific time and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) at that same time, [there is no such contradiction when they belong to different times].
There is no such flaw, because we do not accept ignorance as the cause; rather,
we accept that the cause is simply the knowledge of [the action] being generally achievable through effort and being a means to a desired end, without any further qualifications.
[The author] states that such knowledge is possible, saying "at one time" (*ekadā*).

And this [phrase] is connected with the word "knowledge," because knowledge arises from knowledge. Since it is an empirical fact that even for a tree whose roots and so forth are not perceived, there is the cognition "it is conjoined," there is knowledge of a non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*).

It should be noted that there is no evidence for the restrictive rule that [a cognition] must have only its own delimiting factor as its object; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not apply. He states the view of the modern followers of the Prābhākara school: "The moderns, however," etc.

[He says] "because it is impossible to know," etc., regarding the absence of perception [of universals] if the universal-characterized means of proximity (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*) is not accepted.

The meaning is that inference is impossible due to the absence of knowledge of the *pakṣa* (the subject). Because of that absence, there is an absence of the knowledge that "this person is like one for whom it was observed that something is achievable through effort. Now, if the cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) were the generator of activity, then it would follow that activity would occur even toward the future status of crown prince (*yauvarājya*). Therefore—
He said: "But this must be understood."
